section.title: An Approved Workman
section.sectionRationale: Paul turns from endurance to the handling of the word itself. Timothy is to be a workman approved by God, accurately cutting a straight path through the word of truth, over against those whose empty talk spreads like gangrene and whose false teaching upends the faith of some. God's firm foundation still stands, and in a great house there are vessels for honor and for dishonor, so Timothy must cleanse himself, flee youthful passions, and correct opponents with gentleness that leaves room for repentance.
section.thesis: The Lord's approved workman rightly handles the word of truth and refuses corrosive controversy, resting on God's unshakable foundation, cleansing himself to be a vessel fit for honorable use, and gently correcting opponents in hope that God will grant them repentance and rescue from the devil's snare.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the approved workman who rightly handles the word against ruinous word-battles; empty chatter that spreads like gangrene, and God's firm foundation that stands; the great house and its vessels for honor and dishonor; and the Lord's servant who corrects opponents gently, hoping for their repentance.

verses.text: Remind the believers of these things, charging them before God to avoid quarreling over words, which succeeds only in leading the listeners to ruin.
Make every effort to present yourself {{dokimos|approved}} to God, an unashamed workman who {{orthotomeo|accurately handles}} the word of truth.

units.label: Gangrene and a firm foundation
units.note: error spreads, but God's seal stands

verses.text: But avoid irreverent, empty chatter, which will only lead to more ungodliness,
and the talk of such men will spread like {{gangraina|gangrene}}. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus,
who have deviated from the truth. They say that the resurrection has already occurred, and they undermine the faith of some.
Nevertheless, God's firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: “The Lord knows those who are His,” and, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord must turn away from iniquity.”

units.label: Vessels for honor
units.note: cleansed and useful to the Master

verses.text: A large house contains not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay. Some indeed are for honorable use, but others are for common use.
So if anyone cleanses himself of what is unfit, he will be a {{skeuos|vessel}} for honor: sanctified, useful to the Master, and prepared for every good work.
Flee from youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, together with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart.
But reject foolish and ignorant speculation, for you know that it breeds quarreling.
And a {{doulos|servant}} of the Lord must not be quarrelsome, but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, and forbearing.
He must gently reprove those who oppose him, in the hope that God may grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth.
Then they will come to their senses and escape the snare of the devil, who has taken them captive to his will.

dokimos.gloss: Approved after testing, shown to be genuine, like metal proved by fire or a coin found to be true. Timothy is to present himself approved to God, seeking God's verdict rather than human applause. The word implies scrutiny passed, and it stands in pointed contrast to the false teachers who in chapter 3 are called adokimos, disqualified.

orthotomeo.gloss: Literally to cut straight, to make a straight path or cut a straight furrow. Applied to Scripture it means to handle the word accurately, keeping a straight course through it without twisting or veering. The approved workman drives a straight road through the word of truth, rightly dividing and applying it rather than distorting it for empty debate.

gangraina.gloss: Gangrene, the medical term for tissue that rots and spreads, killing what it touches. Paul uses it for false teaching: empty, godless chatter is not harmless talk but a spreading infection that consumes faith. The vivid image explains the urgency of avoiding it and cutting it off before it eats through the body of the church.

skeuos.gloss: A vessel, container, or instrument, an item of household use. In a large house some vessels are for honorable use and some for common tasks. Paul applies the picture to people: whoever cleanses himself from what is unfit becomes a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the Master, ready for every good work.

doulos.gloss: A slave or bondservant, one wholly owned by and devoted to a master. The Lord's servant is defined not by cleverness in argument but by character: not quarrelsome but kind, able to teach, patient, and gentle. Because he belongs to the Lord, his manner toward opponents must reflect his Master's own patient kindness.

basic.context: Paul warns Timothy against the pointless word-fights that were damaging the church and calls him instead to handle Scripture rightly, as a workman God approves. False teaching, like the claim that the resurrection had already happened, was spreading like an infection. Yet God's foundation is secure. Paul urges Timothy to keep himself clean, run from harmful desires, and correct those who oppose the truth gently, hoping God will bring them to repentance.
basic.hermeneutics: The central command is to handle the word of truth accurately, which sets a standard for all faithful Bible teaching: cut a straight path, do not twist it. The passage also models how to deal with error and with those caught in it, firmly rejecting the falsehood while treating people with patient kindness.
basic.originalLanguages: Timothy is to be dokimos, approved after testing, and to orthotomeo, to cut straight, the word of truth. False talk spreads like gangraina, gangrene. In the great house some are a skeuos, a vessel, for honor. And the Lord's doulos, servant or slave, must be gentle, correcting opponents in hope of their repentance.
basic.typology: The great house with its vessels pictures the church, a mixed community now, sorted at last into honorable and common use. God's sealed foundation recalls the temple built on a sure cornerstone, fulfilled in Christ.
basic.christ: The word of truth Timothy handles is the gospel of Christ, and the resurrection the false teachers distorted is the hope secured by Christ's own rising. God's firm foundation with its double seal rests on the Lord who knows His own and calls them to holiness.
basic.god: God approves genuine workers, knows those who are truly His, and holds His foundation firm no matter how error spreads. He is the Master served by honorable vessels, and He alone grants repentance that leads people out of the devil's trap.
basic.crossReferences: First Timothy 1 also names Hymenaeus among those whose faith was shipwrecked. First Corinthians 15 defends the future bodily resurrection the false teachers denied. Numbers 16 stands behind the seal, the Lord knows those who are His.
basic.oneStory: God is building a people on a foundation that cannot be shaken, sealed as His own and called to holiness. Error will spread and some will fall away, but the Lord knows His own, and He uses cleansed, gentle servants to reclaim the wandering, moving His story toward a purified people fit for the Master's use.

context.literary:
This passage is built on a pair of opposites, words that destroy and the Word handled rightly. It opens and closes in the same territory of speech. Verses 14 to 18 deal with talk that ruins its hearers, and verses 23 to 26 return to quarrelsome speculation, but now the answer is a servant who speaks gently. Between those frames sits the sealed foundation of verse 19 and the picture of the great house in verses 20 and 21, so the whole thing reads as a sandwich: bad talk, God's secure ground, a lesson about cleansing, and then bad talk again with a remedy.

Paul's commands to Timothy alternate between what to do and what to avoid. 'Remind' and 'make every effort' are matched by 'avoid' in verse 16 and 'reject' in verse 23. In verses 22 and 23 the pattern is compressed: flee, pursue, reject. This is the language of a path with a clear direction, and it prepares for the final verses, where the servant who has been walking it is asked to bring others back.

The single vivid image of the passage is the gangrene of verse 17. It is brief, and it explains why Paul treats empty talk as a medical emergency. The other images are structural. The 'foundation' with its inscription is architecture, the 'great house' is domestic life, and the 'snare' of verse 26 is the language of hunting. Paul moves between a building, a household and a trap, each time to show a different side of the same danger.

Two names, Hymenaeus and Philetus, anchor the abstract warning in a real case. The seal's two sentences, one about God's knowing and one about the believer's turning away, are carefully balanced, so that divine initiative and human responsibility stand next to each other in the same inscription.
context.historical:
The 'quarreling over words' that Paul fears belongs to the church in Ephesus, where Timothy was left to deal with teachers who loved speculation, myths and genealogies, 1 Timothy 1:3-7 and Titus 1:11. A word fight in that context was not a harmless debate. It could pull whole households away from the faith. Paul says these teachers 'undermine entire households,' and the picture of gangrene in verse 17 fits an error that spreads silently from person to person through ordinary conversation.

The particular error was that 'the resurrection has already occurred.' Greek thought in general was uncomfortable with the idea that the body would be raised, and Paul met mockery of the doctrine in Athens, Acts 17:32. It was easy for teachers influenced by that atmosphere to turn Paul's own language about being raised with Christ, Colossians 3:1 and Ephesians 2:5-6, into a purely spiritual event already over. That reading would leave no place for a bodily rising at the end, and no hope for the body, so it would tear the heart out of the gospel, 1 Corinthians 15:17-19.

Hymenaeus appears also in 1 Timothy 1:19-20, where he is among those who have shipwrecked their faith and whom Paul has 'handed over to Satan.' That detail shows the problem had been confronted before, and that it was still alive when Paul wrote. Philetus is named only here.

The house of verse 20 would have been a familiar sight in a wealthy household. Expensive tableware of gold and silver was for guests, while wood and clay vessels served for ordinary needs. Paul uses the contrast not to make a snobbish point but to describe how a household has different kinds of containers, some for display and some for ordinary use, and then to place the responsibility for becoming fit for honor on the one who cleanses himself.
context.canonical:
The seal of verse 19 quotes the Old Testament. 'The Lord knows those who are His' draws on Numbers 16:5, where Moses tells Korah and his followers that the LORD will show who belongs to Him. The second line, a call to turn from iniquity, matches Moses' warning in Numbers 16:26 to move away from the tents of wicked men. So the story of Korah's rebellion lies behind the verse, with the same sorting of the true from the false and the same demand for separation. Isaiah 52:11, 'Depart, depart... purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the LORD,' stands behind the call for cleansing in verse 21.

The 'foundation' recalls Isaiah 28:16, where God lays in Zion 'a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation,' and the believer 'will never be shaken.' The New Testament reads this of Christ in 1 Peter 2:4-6 and of the church in Ephesians 2:19-22, which says the household of God is built on the apostles and prophets with Christ Jesus as the cornerstone. In 1 Corinthians 3:11 Paul says no one can lay any foundation other than Christ, and in 1 Timothy 3:15 he calls the church 'the pillar and foundation of the truth.'

The vessels of honor and dishonor are used by Paul in Romans 9:21 for potters and clay, and in 2 Corinthians 4:7 of the treasure in jars of clay. Gentleness toward opponents comes from Jesus, who is 'gentle and humble in heart,' Matthew 11:29, and who fulfils the servant of Isaiah 42:1-3 who will not quarrel or break a bruised reed, Matthew 12:19-20. The hope that errant believers will be won back follows James 5:19-20 and Galatians 6:1, where those who stray are to be restored in a spirit of gentleness.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants Timothy to understand that handling the truth well and treating people well are one task, not two. The first half of the passage is aimed at the truth: avoid pointless fights, work to be approved, and refuse the talk that spreads like gangrene. The second half is aimed at the people: be gentle with those who oppose, be patient, and look for repentance. A leader who has only the first will be sound and harsh. A leader with only the second will be kind and loose. Paul asks for both.

He also wants Timothy to be calm about error. Hymenaeus and Philetus have wrecked some people's faith, yet verse 19 begins with 'Nevertheless.' God's foundation stands, and it carries its own inscription. The danger is real, but it does not mean the church is falling. This is meant to steady Timothy so that he will not respond in panic or bitterness.

Finally, Paul wants Timothy to take responsibility for his own condition. 'If anyone cleanses himself' places the weight on Timothy to be fit for use. The great house will contain every kind of vessel, so Timothy will not get a perfect church, but he can choose which kind of vessel he is. The pursuit of righteousness, faith, love and peace 'together with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart,' verse 22, makes clear that this is not a solitary project.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The account of Hymenaeus and Philetus describes what some people were teaching, and Paul does not endorse it. We should not conclude from it that every claim about resurrection that differs from our own is fatal, or that every error is a gangrene to be cut away at once. The text speaks of a specific teaching that cut at the root of the gospel, and Paul's own reaction is measured: a warning to avoid empty talk, and patient correction of those who oppose.

The great house is a description of the church's mixed condition, and it is wrong to turn it into an instruction to sort the vessels. Timothy is told to cleanse himself, not to draw up a list of who is gold and who is clay. In the same way the vessel language of verse 20 should not be turned into an argument that some people are born with less value. Paul speaks of use, not of worth.

The commands are clear and apply today: work to be approved, handle the word accurately, avoid quarrels over words, flee youthful passions, pursue righteousness, and correct opponents gently. The principle of 'cutting straight' applies to anyone who teaches, whether in a pulpit, a classroom or a kitchen.

debates.question: What did Hymenaeus and Philetus mean by saying the resurrection had already occurred?

views.label: A spiritual resurrection only, already experienced
views.case: The commonest view holds that they took Paul's language of being raised with Christ, Colossians 2:12 and Ephesians 2:5-6, as the whole of the resurrection hope. On their view, new life in Christ is the only resurrection, which leaves no future raising of the body. Paul's response in 1 Corinthians 15, where a bodily rising is the heart of the gospel, would be the answer.

views.label: An early form of the later idea that matter is bad
views.case: Some see in this an early sign of a way of thinking that treated the body as something to escape, so that salvation meant release from the material world. The idea that the resurrection had already happened fits a view in which nothing more needs to come. The exact connection to later movements is debated, and Paul gives no more detail.

views.label: A misreading of the end times
views.case: A smaller group suggests they were saying that the events of the last days had already been fulfilled, such as the general resurrection of Daniel 12:2, and that nothing remained to be waited for. This would also unsettle a church living in hope, but it has less direct support in the text.

debates.bearing: Paul does not say exactly what they taught, only that it overturned faith. What he treats as certain is the reality of the future resurrection, which is why he calls the teaching a deviation from the truth. We should say only as much about their view as the text allows.

debates.question: What does 'cleanses himself of what is unfit' refer to in verse 21?

views.label: Separation from false teachers
views.case: The Greek says 'cleanses himself from these,' and the nearest plural referent is the dishonorable vessels, the false teachers of verses 17 and 18. On this reading Timothy is told to keep his distance from those who spread error, in line with Numbers 16:26 and Isaiah 52:11.

views.label: Cleansing from sin and from error
views.case: Others take 'these' more broadly as the whole range of unfit things, the speculations, quarrels and youthful desires of verses 22 and 23. The cleansing is then moral and doctrinal and does not require Timothy to leave the church. This fits the next verse, which names passions to be fled.

views.label: Both
views.case: A common middle view says the verse covers both, since the two cannot be separated in practice. Anyone who sits close to false teaching will usually find his own heart affected.

debates.bearing: Either way, the cleansing is Timothy's action and the result is usefulness to the Master. Care is needed that this is not read as permission to leave a church at the first sign of weakness, since the same passage tells Timothy to correct opponents gently.

debates.question: Whose will are the captives carrying out in verse 26?

views.label: The devil's will
views.case: The most natural reading is that those caught in the snare have been taken alive by the devil to do what he wants, which fits the picture of a trapped animal and the warnings of 1 Timothy 3:7.

views.label: God's will
views.case: The Greek has two different pronouns, one for 'him' who captured them and a distinct one in 'his will.' Some argue the second points to God, so that the captives are caught by the devil but come to their senses to do God's will. The ambiguity in the Greek is real and the translation is not settled.

debates.bearing: The main point is unaffected. They are captives who can come to their senses, and the means is God's grant of repentance.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul begins with a compound verb, logomacheo, 'to fight over words.' The noun form logomachia appears in 1 Timothy 6:4, and Paul says in both places that it breeds strife. He is not against careful discussion; he has just asked Timothy to teach. The verb describes a battle in which words are the weapon and winning is the aim. The result, katastrophe, is 'ruin' in the sense of an overturning, and the listeners are the ones whose faith is overturned.

In verse 15 'approved' is dokimos, the word for something that has been tested and passed, as a metal is tested for purity. It is used in Romans 14:18 and 16:10, and James 1:12 speaks of 'the one who has stood the test.' The opposite, adokimos, will be the word for the opponents in 2 Timothy 3:8, which is why this passage sets up the next. The worker is an ergates, a labourer; Paul chose a plain word of manual work, not a title of dignity. 'Unashamed' (anepaischyntos) is found in the New Testament only here, and it recalls the shame of chapter 1.

The verb orthotomeo, rendered 'accurately handles,' literally means to cut straight. It appears in the New Testament only here. The Septuagint uses it in Proverbs 3:6, 'He will make your paths straight,' and Proverbs 11:5, so the sense is of making a road go straight, not of dividing the Bible into portions. The workman's task is to keep the message on its true line and not bend it. 'Handles' gives the right idea of skilled, careful work.

In verse 17 'gangrene' is gangraina, a spreading ulcer or cancer, and the word is found only here in the New Testament. The Greek verb for 'spread' has the sense of grazing or feeding, so the image is of an infection that eats its way through a body. In verse 18 'deviated' is astocheo, to miss the mark, used also of those who have wandered from faith in 1 Timothy 1:6 and 6:21. The verb for 'undermine' is anatrepo, to overturn, which Titus 1:11 uses of those who 'undermine entire households.'

The seal in verse 19 is sphragis, an engraved mark of ownership and authenticity. 'Firm' is stereos, hard and stable. The household of verse 20 uses skeuos, a vessel or container, and the pair 'honorable' and 'common' (timē and atimia) is the same as in Romans 9:21. 'Useful' in verse 21, euchrestos, is the word Paul uses of Mark in 2 Timothy 4:11, where Mark, once a failure, has become useful to Paul.

In verse 25 'gently reprove' is paideuo, to train or discipline, from the same family as the 'training in righteousness' of 3:16. The verse says 'if perhaps' God may grant repentance, so Paul does not treat the outcome as guaranteed. In verse 26 'come to their senses' is literally to become sober again, from the family of nepho, and 'taken captive' is zogreo, to take alive, as in Luke 5:10.

typology.type: Korah's rebellion and the seal, Numbers 16
typology.fulfillment: Korah and his company challenged Moses' leadership and were sorted out by the LORD, who made known who was His. The people were told to move away from the tents of the wicked, Numbers 16:26, and the earth swallowed those who stayed, 16:30-33. Paul puts the same lines on the seal of God's foundation. The false teachers of Ephesus are in the position of Korah, and Timothy is in the position of Moses, called to guard the community from error. The escalation is that the 'congregation' is now the church of the living God, 1 Timothy 3:15. The type falls short because the judgment on Korah was immediate and physical, while the judgment on Hymenaeus and Philetus is left with God, and Timothy is told to reprove, not to call down fire.

typology.type: The foundation stone in Zion, Isaiah 28:16
typology.fulfillment: God promised to lay a tested cornerstone in Zion on which believers would rest and not be shaken. The New Testament sees Christ in that stone, 1 Peter 2:4-6, and the church as the building fitted together on Him, Ephesians 2:19-22. Paul's picture of 'God's firm foundation' with its seal carries the same promise: no error can undermine what God has set. The pattern is partly fulfilled now, since the church is on the foundation but still under construction, and it falls short wherever the building is thought of as complete before the Master returns.

typology.type: The house with vessels of gold, silver, wood and clay
typology.fulfillment: In Israel's temple, vessels of gold and silver were set apart for sacred use, and Isaiah 52:11 calls those who carry them to purify themselves. Paul applies this to the church as the great house in which God's people serve. In Christ, every believer is set apart, and Paul uses the picture to say that holiness is the condition of being useful. The correspondence is limited, because a temple vessel does not choose to be cleansed, whereas Timothy is told to cleanse himself. Paul also reminds the Corinthians that the treasure is held in jars of clay, 2 Corinthians 4:7, so clay is not necessarily shameful.

The servant of the LORD in Isaiah 42:1-3 does not quarrel, cry out or break a bruised reed, but brings justice faithfully. Matthew applies this to Jesus in 12:19-20. Timothy, as 'a servant of the Lord,' is asked to take on the same character: not quarrelsome, kind and patient. The escalation is that what Isaiah promised for the Chosen One is now asked, in a lesser measure, of all who serve Him, and it is made possible by His Spirit. The comparison breaks down where the servant of Isaiah is also the one who will bear sin, Isaiah 53, which no human servant can do.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ most directly through the resurrection. The false teachers' claim that the resurrection has already occurred is dangerous because it takes away something the gospel needs, a risen Christ whose rising begins a harvest still to come. Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15:20 that Christ 'has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' and that if He has not been raised, faith is futile, verse 17. The pattern of firstfruits implies more to come. A resurrection that is already over leaves no hope for the body and no meaning for the Lord's own empty tomb.

The foundation is also Christ. Paul calls it 'God's firm foundation,' and elsewhere says no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, 'which is Jesus Christ,' 1 Corinthians 3:11. The cornerstone of Isaiah 28:16 is the stone that Peter says is rejected by men but precious to God, 1 Peter 2:4-6. The seal on the foundation is God's guarantee that those who belong to Christ will not be lost, and John 10:14 says that the Good Shepherd knows His sheep. The first line of the seal, 'The Lord knows those who are His,' is quite at home on the lips of the Lord Jesus.

Christ appears again in the character of the servant. The qualities Paul lists, not quarrelsome, kind, able to teach and forbearing, are the character of Jesus, who says 'I am gentle and humble in heart,' Matthew 11:29, and of whom Matthew writes that 'He will not quarrel or cry out,' 12:19. When Paul pleads with the Corinthians by 'the mildness and gentleness of Christ,' 2 Corinthians 10:1, he is pointing to the same pattern. The Lord's servants are asked to be like the Lord.

The 'Master' of verse 21 is the one who uses the clean vessel. The Greek word is despotes, a master with full authority over a household, and here it points to the Lord, as in Jude 4 and 2 Peter 2:1, where Christ is the Master who bought His people. He is the one who prepares His people for every good work, and who gives repentance. The cleansing of verse 21 is Timothy's task, but it only makes sense because of the cleansing Christ has done. Titus 2:14 says He gave Himself to redeem us from all wickedness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, and the believer's cleansing of himself is a response to that.

There is a safeguard to keep. The passage does not teach that Christ's saving work depends on how well Timothy cleans himself or how patiently he reproves. The one who is approved, as the earlier chapters showed, is approved because of Christ. And the repentance of opponents is something God 'may grant,' not something Timothy's gentleness earns. The servant works, and the Lord brings the change.
study.god:
The first thing this passage shows about God is that He is a builder whose work does not collapse. 'God's firm foundation stands.' The sentence comes straight after the news that some have lost their faith, and it is placed there on purpose. Human teachers can fail, and some who seemed to be part of the church may fall away, but the structure rests on God and is held up by Him. This is both a comfort and a limit. It does not say that every person who joins the church is secure, but that God's own purpose cannot be destroyed.

He is the one who knows. 'The Lord knows those who are His' is God's intimate and active knowledge, the kind that Nahum 1:7 describes when it says He cares for those who trust in Him, and John 10:14 when Jesus says He knows His sheep. The difference between a visible church and the true people of God is known to God even when it is hidden from everyone else. Because God knows, Timothy does not have to be the judge of every heart.

He is holy and calls for holiness. The second line of the seal says that everyone who names the Lord's name must turn from wrongdoing. Calling on God is not a label; it is a commitment with ethical content. The cleansing of verse 21 is the response of a person who has seen that he is called to serve a holy Master. In worship this means that praise and purity belong together.

He is the one who grants repentance. Timothy may reprove and teach, but verse 25 says 'God may grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth.' The Bible treats repentance as both a command and a gift, as in Acts 11:18, where the church glorifies God because He has granted even the Gentiles repentance unto life. Romans 2:4 says that His kindness leads to repentance. The same God who gives the command also gives the ability, which is why gentleness is the right posture, because no one's hardness is beyond Him.

He is also the God who wins. The devil has taken captives, but God brings them to their senses. The image of the snare is balanced by Psalm 124:7, where those who have escaped say 'the net is torn, and we have slipped away.' The enemy is real, as 1 Peter 5:8 and 2 Corinthians 2:11 warn, but his hold is limited and can be broken. God is not merely defending a position; He is recovering prisoners.

Finally, He is the God of truth. The 'word of truth,' verse 15, is His own, and John 17:17 says 'Your word is truth.' The passage's concern for handling it accurately flows from the character of its Author. A God who does not lie gives a word that can be trusted, and to bend it is to treat Him lightly. This is why careful interpretation is an act of worship and not only of scholarship.

crossReferences.note: Shows what Timothy was left in Ephesus to do: stop certain men from teaching false doctrines and from devoting themselves to myths and endless speculation. It gives the background for 'quarreling over words' and shows that the problem in 2 Timothy 2 was long standing.

Names Hymenaeus, with Alexander, among those who have shipwrecked their faith and been handed over to Satan to learn not to blaspheme. It shows that the Hymenaeus of verse 17 had been disciplined before, and that Paul's concern for restoration appears even in an act of judgment.

Paul's fullest defence of the bodily resurrection, written to people who said there was no resurrection of the dead. It is the proper reply to Hymenaeus and Philetus: if Christ has not been raised, faith is futile, and because He has, those who sleep in Him will rise.

Moses tells Korah that in the morning the LORD will show who belongs to Him and who is holy. This is the source of the first line on the seal in verse 19, and it ties Paul's warning about false teachers to Israel's story of a rebellion in which God made the difference plain.

Moses warns the congregation to move away from the tents of these wicked men. It stands behind the second line of the seal, the call to turn away from iniquity, and shows that separation from those who lead others astray was already a theme in Israel's history.

God lays a tested, precious cornerstone in Zion, and the one who believes will never be shaken. It supplies the picture of a firm foundation, and 1 Peter 2:4-6 reads it of Christ. Paul's 'firm foundation' in verse 19 carries the same promise of permanence.

Uses the potter and clay and asks whether the potter has the right to make one vessel for special occasions and another for common use. It shares the vessel language of verse 20, but in Romans the point is God's freedom, while in 2 Timothy 2 the point is human cleansing.

Calls those who carry the vessels of the LORD to depart from uncleanness and purify themselves. It forms the background for verse 21 and adds the notion that those who serve God's house must be clean.

Tells the spiritual to restore someone caught in a trespass with a spirit of gentleness, while watching themselves. It matches the call in verses 24 and 25 to correct opponents gently, and adds the warning that the corrector can fall as well.

Quotes Isaiah's servant who will not quarrel or cry out and will not break a bruised reed. It explains why Paul describes the Lord's servant as not quarrelsome and kind, because the character asked of Timothy is first the character of Jesus.

Describes the elder who holds the faithful word so that he can encourage with sound teaching and refute those who contradict it, and the many who undermine entire households. It joins the two tasks of 2 Timothy 2, firmness toward error and care for people.
Says that whoever brings back one who wanders from the truth will save his soul from death. It gives the positive goal behind verses 25 and 26: the aim of correction is rescue, not victory.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible begins with a word and the lie that twists it. 'Did God really say?' was the first question of the serpent, and from that point on the human race has been prone to bend what God has said. This passage lies in that long line. The false teachers of Ephesus are the latest in a series that includes the serpent of Genesis 3, the false prophets of Israel and the opponents of Jesus. Paul's answer is not novelty but faithfulness to the word. A worker who 'cuts straight' is one who does not bend what God said back toward what people want to hear.

The passage answers the question of how God's people survive when error and failure are present inside the community. In Israel the answer was often sorting: Korah's company was separated from the congregation, Numbers 16, and the prophets called a remnant out. In the New Testament the church is the household of God and the pillar of truth, but it contains people of all kinds. The seal of verse 19 says that God's foundation stands and that He knows His own, even when the visible community looks mixed. This keeps the story from being a tale of constant defeat, since the people of God are secure because of who holds them.

It also sets up the closing chapters of the letter. The warning about opponents in chapter 3, the coming of those who will not endure sound teaching in chapter 4, and the last charge to preach the word all develop what is begun here. The 'approved workman' of chapter 2 is contrasted with the 'disqualified' men of chapter 3, and Timothy is held between them.

The passage makes the story personal by describing God's way of dealing with those who are captured. The enemy has them in a snare, and the remedy is not a campaign but a servant who reproves with gentleness in the hope that God will grant repentance. This follows the pattern of the cross, where the way God conquers evil is by patient love, not by force. The Messiah of Isaiah 42 who will not break a bruised reed is the one who leads justice to victory.

The end of the story is a household in which every vessel is fit for the Master's use. Revelation 21 shows a city foursquare on twelve foundations, with the names of the apostles of the Lamb on them, and nothing unclean will ever enter. The foundation laid in Zion is the foundation of the new Jerusalem. On that day the seal on the foundation is read to the full, as the Lord who knew His own gathers them in, and the snare of the devil is gone for good, Revelation 20:10. The word handled with care in Ephesus will be the word that has proved true.

sermon.title: Pastor and People
sermon.why: Part of Begg's series A Study in 2 Timothy, this message expounds 2 Timothy 2:14-15, the call to avoid ruinous quarrels over words and to be an approved workman who accurately handles the word of truth, setting the standard for faithful, careful handling of Scripture.

quiz.q: What does it mean to be an approved workman who accurately handles the word of truth?

options.text: To interpret and teach Scripture accurately, cutting a straight path through it.
options.note: The image is cutting straight, handling the word without twisting it.

options.text: To win as many arguments about words as possible.
options.note: Paul condemns quarreling over words as leading to ruin.

options.text: To reshape Scripture to fit what listeners want to hear.
options.note: That is the crooked handling Paul warns against, not straight cutting.

options.text: To handle God's word with care and integrity so it runs true.
options.note: True and close, though the specific image is cutting a straight path through the word.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe the effect of empty, godless chatter?

options.text: It spreads like gangrene, corroding faith wherever it goes.
options.note: Verse 17 uses the medical image of spreading rot.

options.text: It is harmless talk that does no lasting damage.
options.note: Paul treats it as a deadly, spreading infection.

options.text: It leads only to more ungodliness.
options.note: True from verse 16, though the vivid picture is the spreading gangrene.

options.text: It is a minor issue best simply ignored.
options.note: Paul takes it seriously and names offenders; it must be avoided, not shrugged off.

quiz.q: What double seal marks God's firm foundation in verse 19?

options.text: The Lord knows those who are His, and His people must turn from iniquity.
options.note: The seal joins God's electing knowledge with the call to holiness.

options.text: That the foundation will eventually crumble under false teaching.
options.note: The point is the opposite: it stands firm despite error.

options.text: That God knows and keeps His own people securely.
options.note: True, the first line of the seal, but the second line about turning from iniquity is also part of it.

options.text: That only the most gifted teachers truly belong to God.
options.note: Belonging rests on God knowing His own, not on giftedness.

quiz.q: How does one become a vessel for honorable use in the great house?

options.text: By cleansing oneself from what is unfit, becoming useful to the Master.
options.note: Verse 21 ties honorable use to being cleansed and sanctified.

options.text: By being made of gold or silver rather than wood or clay.
options.note: The material is the picture; the real issue is being cleansed for honorable use.

options.text: By nothing at all; usefulness is fixed and cannot change.
options.note: Paul says anyone who cleanses himself becomes a vessel for honor.

options.text: By separating from what defiles and pursuing holiness.
options.note: True and near, though the verse frames it as cleansing oneself to be useful to the Master.

quiz.q: How is the Lord's servant to treat those who oppose the truth?

options.text: Kindly and gently, correcting them in hope God grants repentance.
options.note: Verses 24 to 25 call for kindness, patience, and gentle correction.

options.text: With sharp quarreling until he wins the argument.
options.note: Paul says the servant must not be quarrelsome.

options.text: By ignoring them completely and never engaging.
options.note: He is to correct them, but gently, not to ignore them.

options.text: Patiently and able to teach, leaving room for God to work.
options.note: True and close, capturing the manner, with the aim being repentance and knowledge of the truth.

questions: Paul prizes accurate handling of Scripture over clever debate. How carefully do you handle the Bible, and where might you be tempted to bend it to suit yourself or win a point?
Empty, godless talk spreads like gangrene. What conversations or content in your life are quietly corroding your faith, and what would it look like to cut them off?
God's foundation stands, sealed by the truth that the Lord knows those who are His. How does resting in God knowing you steady you when error and confusion are all around?
A vessel for honor is one that has been cleansed. What in your life is God asking you to be cleansed from so you can be more useful to the Master?
The Lord's servant corrects opponents with gentleness, hoping for their repentance. Who in your life is opposing the truth, and how might patient kindness serve them better than winning an argument?

translationNotes.note: Some manuscripts read the Lord rather than God in the phrase charging them before God, as the BSB footnote observes; the sense is unchanged.
Accurately handles renders a verb meaning to cut straight, the image of a straight furrow or road driven through the word of truth.
The first line of the seal, the Lord knows those who are His, draws on Numbers 16:5, as the BSB footnote notes; see also the Greek Old Testament.
Cleanses himself of what is unfit is literally cleanses himself of these, referring back to the dishonorable vessels and their corrupting talk, per the BSB footnote.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for 2 Timothy 2:14-26. Curly quotation marks within verse 19 are from the source text.
